items.title: Thoughts on hobbies
items.summary:
There is an optimal intensity range for doing hobbies or anything hobby-related. I suspect this also applies to things outside of hobbies.

For example, if you’re reading a book, there’s a speed that’s too slow: you don’t get immersed enough into the book, you lose track of what it was that you read about last time you read the book, and it’s a sort of a protracted pain, in which the very act of reading the book feels like a chore.

Then on the other end, there’s reading a book too fast. You blaze through it so fast that it doesn’t feel like you savored it enough. It feels like you could have gone a bit slower and enjoyed the process of reading. This applies both to fiction and non-fiction; as a child, I once read Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (~700 pages) in a day, and felt sad because I didn’t get to properly experience the emotional ups and downs. I remember setting the book down in the afternoon and saying to myself: “well, this sucks, I should have taken a week to read this”.

Similarly, I once read Peter Singer’s Practical Ethics (~100) pages for four entire months. It’s not that the book was bad, I just had other things going on in my life and, as a result, it took me a great deal of time to go through a relatively short book. I remember saying to myself: “wow, this took around 10 times longer as it should have”.

In other hobbies that I’ve done: I’ve both done too much jiu jitsu and too little jiu jitsu, in different periods of my life. In the first instance, I was preparing for a tournament, so the extra effort was understandable, but there was a sense in which it had become an obligation, a pain in the ass, something I had to go through because I had previously committed to the idea of competing and representing my club. And in the “too little” era, I’d go once a month, or twice a month, and I’d just feel guilty for not going more, and then the class would progress without me actually building my game in a systematic way.

There’s something rather disheartening when you do too little of your hobby, you get back to it, maybe due to a moment of inspiration, and you try to do the last thing you did when you were actually doing the hobby more frequently, and you realize that you can’t. You’ve regressed. Your skill has dropped considerably and you now have to relearn the thing you sort of mastered a couple of months or years ago.

Every once in a while I’ll pick up the guitar and realize that I always have to relearn the same song (Malaguena). I’ve become really really good at the first 30 seconds of it, and everything after that is a pain to go through. To be clear: I can play it, it just isn’t masterful or fluid, you can hear the stutters and the attempts to remember (except certain passages that I can’t play at all because I never got to them).

I started learning this song… oh, it must be five years or more now. And it’s annoying because after five years of technically trying to learn it, I feel partially like a failure (who takes five years to learn a single song?) but on the other hand I know that if I learned it appropriately – spending a couple of hours a week instead of a couple of hours per quarter – I could probably nail it in, I don’t know, a week or two. I give myself a month for proper mastery.

The “doing a hobby too rarely” thing stings even more when it’s a social hobby like the aforementioned jiu jitsu, because you train alongside guys who are roughly at your skill level. Then you go off and do whatever you do in your life that makes you not adhere to a reasonable training schedule of three sessions a week, you start coming in once a week, then once a month, then you skip a couple of months. And once you decide “ok it’s time to actually come back”, you meet with the same guys that were on your own level, or even below, such that you were regularly beating them, and you just get crushed.

This is all a tradeoff between width and breadth; you can’t do everything, and you can’t get better at everything at the same time, and you can only get good at a limited amount of things anyway, because to remain good, for any definition of “good”, it takes continuous investment of time and energy. Obviously this only applies to hobbies where there is a skill ladder, but most hobbies are like that. I guess some people do things for enjoyment alone. Listening to music and going for walks are such activities. You can’t really become better at listening to music or better at having a walk. Yet even in those situations I will find myself exploring the edges of that activity. I’ll try to figure out a piece of music, or I’ll listen to more bands or more obscure genres, sort of “expanding” my listening repertoire, and thereby improving my taste. Same for “going for a walk”, the most harmless, non-competitive, enjoyment-only hobby, I will at the very least try to map out my neighborhood, see as much as I can of any given place, explore different trails, and then I’ll really go overboard and start rucking (putting a weighted rucksack and doing more of a military march than a relaxed walk).

One thing that does bring me comfort is that sometimes explicitly setting a hobby to “maintenance only” brings a sort of peace of mind. It’s like: I no longer wish to improve my skill in this area, and I am satisfied with doing the minimum work necessary not to lose all progress that I have accumulated.

Another thing is redefining the goal of the hobby. I keep going back to jiu jitsu but it probably applies to many other hobbies; I have redefined my whole game to ignore 90% of any standard jiu jitsu curriculum, instead focusing only on Just Standing Up ™️ in every single situation, doing a couple of mount escapes, having almost no offense, and literally only two or three strangles, with zero locks of any kind. My “game”, if it can be even called that way, is so stripped down to bare essentials that it would have looked silly to me from seven years ago, but here I am, discarding almost all of the curriculum because I have redefined the goal of what the activity means to me: I want to be able to stand up in any single situation, I want to never be pinned down, and if I do attack, I want to do only attacks that work against bigger opponents with very high pain tolerance (even pain-resistant heavyweights will go to sleep from a stranglehold). This is similar to my current drumming “game”, where I don’t really care about fills or… whatever you’re supposed to be learning. I just focus on hi-hat-snare-bass, turn on my metronome, and build up my precision and grooviness (this is even visible in how much less wear and tear there is on the rest of the drum kit).

Finally a third thing is learning that there is indeed such a range, where doing anything below or above it will have its own set of problems. This will allow me to say “no” to many things, which will help me concentrate my energy on one thing, doing it well rather than watering down my efforts by doing too many things poorly. This has paid off the most I think. I’ll give anything a go, really, but I will not give a second go to most things. I’ve thus far successfully evaded three attempts to be recruited into a band, a tennis school, and a skiing trip.

items.title: The Dark Side of Being Highly Ambitious
items.content_html:
Share

Being highly ambitious is trendy right now.

Everyone wants to be a high performer. They froth at the mouth over tweets like “Join the top 1%.” The traditional career economy is collapsing at the same time.

9-5 jobs are out of fashion. Promotions are faraway dreams. Salary increases are rare. Everyone has a better job than you. Layoffs are a permanent “F you, you could be fired tomorrow, so get into line or you’re gone, pal.”

No one trusts big corporations anymore. They’ve lied to us for too long.

This reality has led people to either give up or become highly ambitious. Being highly ambitious seems like a blue pill from the Matrix that you swallow and unlock some kind of computer game cheat code. And it can be.

But…

Being highly ambitious has a dark side, and you should know what that is before you go any further. Let me explain through my life and the lives of many other highly ambitious people I spend time with inside of high-end masterminds.

A soul-crushing sense of loneliness

Everyone loves being highly ambitious.

No one is prepared for the loneliness that comes with it. When you dedicate your entire life to a big goal, normal people stop understanding you. I go to picnics and kids’ birthday parties with my 3 year old. You’d think it’d be fun. Not really.

I feel this deep sense of loneliness.

Everyone wants to talk about normie sh*t that doesn’t matter. No one wants to talk about the meaning of life. Or how they’re going to run an ultramarathon and win a gold medal. Very few people have big goals.

They’re just happy settling for second best and being told what to do.

When their country or way of life comes under threat they’re too comfortable to do anything about it. They sit there and just watch society crumble without feeling any sense of duty or aspiration to make a difference.

Being highly ambitious makes you different.

That difference starts out as cool and eventually becomes loneliness. You find yourself locked in a spare bedroom at home doing work no one understands. Or never seeing high school or university friends ever again.

You can go days without seeing anyone at all. You can live the same day on repeat for a year and not feel bad about it. Life becomes seasons. Life becomes a series of marathons that you run without looking back.

Some days you feel like you don’t have a friend in the world. You just exist for the mission.

Long hours that’ll rip your face off

Hard work has lost all its meaning.

One side of society demonises hard work and calls it hustle culture, so they can sit at home and have bubble baths without feeling guilty. The other half of society worships hard work like a false god.

Highly ambitious people have a different relationship with hard work.

They know it’s necessary and they’ve come to terms with it. They don’t worship it. They simply see it as part of the game. You can’t be ambitious and achieve big goals without hard work. And there are consequences to this reality that are rarely spoken.

Hard work means long hours. That means less time with your loved ones. During some seasons of life, it means working 7 days a week or staying up way past your bedtime. The other night I had an urgent project and only slept 6 hours.

I knew it was bad but that’s the dark side of ambition. You’re willing to make sacrifices. You’re willing to do what it takes because the mission becomes bigger than the individual the more you let ambition take over. This reality may not be a good thing, but it is the reality.

Recently, people made fun of creator Dan Koe on X.com.

One user posted a photo of him 3 years ago compared to now. Back then he looked like a baby-faced kid. Now, some say he looks like a 40 year old man, yet he’s still in his 20s.

The difference in the photos is hours worked. I know Dan Koe outside of his online persona. What it might surprise you to know is he works extremely hard. He’s building a software company and letting it consume him.

He thinks about nothing else. He does all-nighters. He neglects his diet at times.

The mission is bigger than him. He’s prepared to accept the trade-offs and have people comment on his appearance (a true leader).

That’s what working long hours does to you. It makes you look different. And it may even make a 20 year old look like a 40 year old.

Doing work no one understands

I’ve given up explaining what I do.

I shouldn’t admit this, but half the time I still tell people I’m a banker. It’s just easier to explain. That’s not what I really do. Surface-level people say I do coaching or consulting. Not really.

I’m helping humanity progress back to the old days, where entrepreneurship was the main career and form of work. I’m helping people learn the skills of becoming self-sufficient so they can experience modern freedom.

To achieve this mission I am building a social media machine, that based on its current trajectory, will rival the audience size of someone like Tim Ferriss.

How the heck do I explain that to Bob from my 3 year old’s kinder? I can’t. So I don’t. I’ve given up. It’s too complicated. And it’ll only repel people.

I can’t even explain it to my wife or kids. It’s a mission so deep, personal, and purpose-driven that only I understand it. And I’ve had to come to terms with that.

It’s not easy.

Success can become a form of mental illness

This one’s controversial.

My friend G said something that screwed me up for weeks. He said people like me building big social media followings and embarking on some huge mission are mentally ill. One example he gave was Tim Ferriss.

He reminded me that Tim was molested by his babysitter. Then he borrowed a book in college to learn how to end his own life. Through some bizarre turn of events the book was unavailable and when it came back in stock at the library the reminder letter went to his parent’s home. They saw the book title & knew what Tim was up to.

This saved Tim’s life.

He went on to build multiple highly successful businesses, be a well-known investor in the most successful tech companies in history, and launch a podcast that is one of the biggest in the world.

When you hear him talk about trying to find a wife or having kids one day, it sounds like the words of a psychopath. G reminded me of this. He said the only rational label you can give Tim Ferriss is “mentally ill.”

That’s his opinion. I’m no doctor, but it’s an idea worth thinking about. What if the dark side of being highly ambitious and god forbid “successful” is that you must knowingly become mentally ill?

That’s a dark side few people would want to admit.

Being an undiagnosed neurodivergent person

I hate labels.

And I don’t like being given diagnoses. But I’ve realized my need for tidiness and order is likely a mild form of obsessive compulsive disorder. I’m also likely ADHD, and maybe even autistic.

I don’t think I know a single highly ambitious person who doesn’t have an undiagnosed form of neurodivergence. This is a dark side.

These conditions certainly have downsides. Some days I can’t think. Some days I’m a scatter brain. Some days I’m in such a trance, I unconsciously do weird things like pour coffee in my kid’s sandwich.

I wonder if everyone is a little ADHD or autistic at times.

And whether highly ambitious people are just a little more ADHD or autistic than the regular person. Perhaps it’s not a “you have it” or “you don’t,” but it’s a scale. And the higher you aim to get in life the more neurodivergent you become.

Dark masterminds

Normal society hangs out in pubs and cafes.

Highly ambitious people hang out in private masterminds. To join you’re required to fill out application forms that’d scare most people away – and that have minimum requirements most people don’t meet.

If you hang around in these dark masterminds for long enough, strange things start to happen. In one mastermind I got into, conversations started heading down the path of “deep state.” Even billionaires started to become interested in what we were doing.

Turns out any influence or success you have in a field can start to become interesting to those at the top who want to use it for their personal gain. In my case, it went down a path of overthrowing government which sounds wild to say in public.

I obviously ran from it lol. No thanks.

Decide on what you will and won’t do before you enter the underbelly of masterminds. Have rules. Have morals. And never lose sight of your core vision.

Deep flow states that look bizarre

The typical way to work is in short bursts. Most of the work is done in a distracted state, too, with the phone pinging all day.

When you’re highly ambitious you find yourself working in deep flow states, where hours feel like minutes.

Wild stuff can happen.

One flow state I got stuck in lasted for 16 hours. The entire day felt like a few minutes and it produced some of the best work of my life.

Many of my most popular Substack essays come from going down a rabbit hole and not making it back out until 8+ hours later.

This isn’t normal. And it can be scary.

High ambition transcends the now. It takes you out of reality and into a 3rd dimension that is hard to describe to normal people. Sometimes this world goes so deep you don’t know how you ever got there.

To the outside, it looks like madness. But to you it feels like a force from another world that is pulling you in a certain direction and you can’t ignore it.

Many people thought classical music composer Mozart was mad. He worked at extraordinary speed and could meet even the toughest deadlines. He could even write out a whole symphony in a few days.

Letters show that Mozart was composing in his head while also having conversations with friends and playing billiards. Some say the music was running in the background of his mind at all times, then when he sat down he simply transcribed it.

His entire life ran off these insane flow states. And his flow states became so powerful that the composition became automatic and seemed to require little effort.

Yes, the dark side of flow states is they can last a long time. But they can also allow a highly ambitious person to have so much skill, their work looks effortless.

An insane level of obsession

Highly ambitious people are obsessed.

People think obsession is cool. I’m guilty of sharing that idea. But obsession has a dark side too. Writer Sahil Bloom explains:

The scariest thing in the world is truly going all in on something. Because it strips away every single pre-built excuse you may have for falling short. You’re completely naked. It’s terrifying. But it’s also why all the rewards in life go to those who have the courage to do it.

Highly ambitious people chase their obsession, and when they do, they must act with a delusional sense of optimism. It’s not one-off courage. It’s daily courage.

The downsides or the risks are completely ignored which is why people chasing their obsession are called crazy. The best way to describe obsession is it’s when you go all in. When nothing else matters. When there’s no to-do list. When there’s no Plan B or hedging your bets. You just bet your entire world on one idea.

The process produces dark thoughts, I’m not gonna lie. Sometimes I think I’m going to ruin my family’s life. Or I am going to say something that gets me in a lot of trouble. Obsession is a dance with darkness. It’s an acceptance of chaos at times.

After a while you start to feel a sense of thrill. All the darkness oddly turns into a level of motivation that is hard to describe. It feels like nothing can stop you, and at the same time, something might stop you.

Mostly, you get good at blocking out the dark voices inside your head. And on some days you just let the darkness win and stop fighting it. Your inner dialogue can get wild, and that’s okay. Better than thinking about donuts or Netflix all day.

You shouldn’t trade this for anything

Every goal or action in life has downsides.

Social media life p0rn is full of the bright side, but it rarely covers the dark side. And most people never go to the dark side of being highly ambitious, so they can’t explain it to you. I’ve been there daily for 12 years.

Yes, it’s terrifying at times. At the same time, the dark side of being highly ambitious makes you come alive. It stops you from being dead inside like mainstream society.

I wouldn’t trade the dark parts of being highly ambitious for anything.

It’s part of who I am. It makes me do weird things. And the story it creates is something Hollywood loves to make movies about.

Don’t suppress the dark side of being highly ambitious. Embrace it. See the negatives as positives. Accept the trade-offs, and stay the hell away from the painful depression that is mediocrity.

P.S.

New video just dropped. I’m tackling a major problem people have when starting a digital business.

Most people ask: “What business should I start?”

Honestly not a great question.

Ask this question instead to get faster results starting your digital business.

items.title: Habits I stole from my millionaire boss when I was 33
items.content_html:
Share

It’s weird to work with a boss who doesn’t give a f*ck.

Normally a boss wants to micromanage people, kiss a$$, get promoted, etc. They’re often a company man or woman that’d do anything for their employer.

My banking boss when I was 33 was bizarre.

As I got to know him, I realized the way he treated his job came down to the fact he was a millionaire. He didn’t need the job for money, so this changed his behavior. He was seeking something more.

It took me a while to figure out what.

Because he didn’t need cash, he didn’t take cr*p from anyone. And people didn’t mess with him or his team. He also didn’t sit in back-to-back meetings.

This gave him a lot of extra free time. And it made him extremely zen.

We’d often sit in cafes for hours talking about the meaning of life. Or we’d go to a 6-hour lunch with a client/lead. By the end of lunch the client felt so loved and entertained, the deal practically closed itself.

I’ll never forget this millionaire boss. He changed my life. He gave me the skills and mindset to retire at 34.

Here are the bizarre habits I stole from him that can change your life too.

1. Be quiet in most meetings

Meetings are full of big egos. They want to dominate the conversation.

And this is why not much gets done in big companies. Everyone is so busy fighting and trying to get promoted that nobody listens. I’d go to meetings with my millionaire boss and he wouldn’t say a word. He just took notes, observed, and listened.

This gave him a massive edge.

People didn’t know what he was thinking. And being quiet gave him much higher status.

The loudest people in meetings are the most stupid. Being quiet allows you to be underestimated. Be the Buddhist monk. Be zen. It's much higher status and will give you an aura people can't describe.

2. Stop working with low performers

The masses are low performers.

The world needs low performers so they can get underpaid, get taken advantage of, be laid off at the drop of a hat, and to do all the boring work nobody else wants to do.

Every workplace is drowning in unserious people who live for the weekend and are dying to take another holiday.

Don’t hate on it. Low performance is a fact of life. But if you allow yourself to be in this category, you’ll get screwed because of it.

Stay away from low performers. Their pessimism and laziness is like a virus that’ll drag you down and give you herpes.

Spend time around top performers instead. The more entrepreneurial ones.

The ones who see problems as opportunities. The ones who use their creativity and imagination, instead of working in admin mode all day and drowning in distractions and phone notifications that never stop.

3. Cheat on your job with a side hustle

I was a stupidly loyal “company man.”

I did whatever the bank told me to do, even if I knew it was dumb or bad for the customer. This made me a people-pleasing kiss a**. Yuck. This is the default path if you bet your life on a corporation that can lay you off with one email and zero f*cks.

My millionaire boss acted differently.

He had side hustles, side businesses, offline consulting gigs, and even board positions at other companies. He didn’t hide it either.

He knew that the most successful people in business have multiple interests.

He didn’t let non-competes and HR policies stop him from having other income sources. He just made sure he wasn’t doing anything dumb or stealing bank clients.

And even if it all blew up, he knew no company would bother suing him. Too hard. Not worth it. And the burden of proof is too high.

After he told me all this, I felt like I had a spiritual awakening.

All my fears started to go away. I was afraid of a boogeyman that didn’t exist. I asked my lawyer and friend Robbo and he agreed (not legal advice).

So I changed how I thought about work and my income. It led me to make $70K USD a month on the side.

The smartest workers are all building stuff on the side. They understand a job is how you get underpaid. Great way to start. Dumb strategy to embrace for 40 years.

Your customers & network are the bones of your first business. Act that way. Start building a business long before you need it. See a job as a form of modern slavery, and a one-person business or bigger as a way to become self-sufficient.

You’re probably too smart to work in an adult daycare for the next few decades and follow nanny police rules while getting told what to do by people much dumber than you. And I’m willing to bet you hate commuting to an office. Don’t do it.

4. Always be closing

I freaking love this strategy.

My millionaire boss had a weird obsession with the movie Glengarry Glen Ross, starring Alec Baldwin. The famous line “always be closing” became a mantra.

I later adopted it.

The way he explained it to me is I should always tell management about the offers I’m getting from competitors. I should let them know recruiters are reaching out to me on LinkedIn every day. He told me:

“Always ask for more money, better job titles, bigger teams to lead.”

If you don’t ask you don’t get, and then you starve. Being proactive is crucial. Don’t focus on what you’re doing now. Communicate the vision of where you’re heading. Think and act like a high performer long before you become one.

This strategy allows you to psychologically challenge management the same way they do to you with KPIs and the constant threat of layoffs. It’s a two-way street.

You must brainwash them to understand you’re in demand, getting better offers, and will go where you’re most valued. It’s psychological warfare and it works. I used this strategy to rapidly increase my salary, get bigger bonuses, and even work 4-day weeks.

You get what you negotiate.

5. Ignore 99% of emails

Answering emails is a full-time job for most people.

My millionaire boss replied to very few emails. He saw an email as a request and not an obligation. He had some killer email rules:

  • Never reply to the first email. See if they follow up, which tells you how serious the email is.

  • For legit emails, respond fast.

  • Delete all internal comms.

  • Ignore noise. Don’t have debates in emails.

  • Pick up the phone instead of email if it’s important.

  • Be extremely brief in emails. Save people time. Get to the point.

After I adopted this approach, I spent only a few minutes a day in emails. The rest of the time I was doing productive tasks, like making sales and getting applications approved with the risk team (which is why I outsold everyone else).

6. Say no to most meetings

The wealthiest workers work smart. They have free time to do the real work by ignoring the bullsh*t work.

Meetings are BS. They’re unproductive. Most meetings could have been an email. Wasting time is the aim of the game for corporate. Opt out.

My millionaire boss rarely went to meetings.

He focused his time on being with clients. And he outsourced internal meetings to people below him (like me). Or he just said “I have a customer appointment at that time” and the customer-first mantra that every corporate pretends to adopt would say “Oh, of course. Customers first!”

(Weaponize corporate BS, cliches, and slogans against the system itself.)

If your whole day is full of meetings, you have no time to do the real work. This holds your career back and wastes your life. Fewer meetings, more deep work.

7. Be early to meetings

Makes you look organized. Shows you care. Allows you to build rapport before the meeting. This is crucial in customer meetings. The before-meeting banter is the free networking that closes deals and gets you consulting gigs.

8. Ask your employer's customers for consulting gigs

Some people are going to lose their sh*t in the comments. Good.

This one is a little controversial. It’s one of those underground tactics people in the know use but rarely talk about. This is the first step to migrating to a business owner.

The people most likely to hire you for consulting are your current clients.

The average person doesn’t think like a business so they’d never even entertain this idea. But it’s logical. Your clients at a job probably like and trust you more than strangers, or than sending 1000 DMs to people on LinkedIn.

So, the easiest business to get out of the rat race is just independently consulting to customers you’ve already worked with. In some cases, you can do it while still employed. In other cases, you may need to quit.

The technicalities don’t matter. What matters is the mindset.

One person sees problems and moves at the speed of a snail, so they get trapped in an office pleb job for years. Another person sees their job as a place to build a business and uses all the same resources to build THEIR business.

My millionaire boss taught me the latter. When he later left corporate his first big client was one of our old banking clients.

Our employer knew, but there was nothing they could do. In fact, our employer encouraged him to do it because it still benefited them to have a former employee advocating for their bank on the outside as a consultant.

When you think in terms of incentives, it makes it easier to make moves most would consider too dangerous.

9. Show up with high energy

Because most people are low energy.

They drink too much alcohol. They eat food that makes them feel like sh*t. And they feel tired all the time at work which unknowingly affects their quality of work.

My millionaire boss had high energy. He ate a monk diet of mostly lean meat and vegetables. He drank plenty of water and avoided sugar like the plague. High energy people have aura. They light the room up. And everyone wants to be around them.

Quit coffee. Sleep well. Exercise. Don't become a corporate fat slob.

People don’t buy products and services, they unconsciously buy your energy. High energy feels good. Low energy feels off and makes people skeptical.

10. Become known as a problem solver, not a problem creator

Most employees complain. They create problems. And they refuse to change.

Do the opposite. Solve problems. Become known for it. Tell management about all the problems you solve. My millionaire boss was the ultimate problem solver. He took highly complex problems and broke them down for large teams in 5th grader language.

When our IT systems collapsed, he came up with a genius plan that framed it to our customers as a positive – instead of an outage that cost them money.

When you interview for jobs... lean hard into real problems you solved.

Explain how you did it. Proof of work beats “trust me” and “I have potential dontcha know.” The problems you solve at work later become the same problems you solve as a business owner.

11. Lead small teams as early as possible

The most highly desirable career for a 20 year old is to be a Youtuber.

For people in their 40s like me, the most desirable career is now to be a thought leader using social media. What’s often misunderstood is if you’re going to build any kind of audience online, you need to get strangers to click the “follow” button.

That means you need to be a leader by default.

But the average person isn’t a leader. They’re a coward. They’re full of fear. They’re petrified to do anything other than their job because they are risk-averse. So they have the dream but can’t make it happen because they don’t think and act like a leader.

Cowards don’t become leaders or build businesses.

The antidote is to lead people as early as you can. Leadership is a powerful skill. It forces you to understand other humans. It makes you more valuable. Oh, and makes you more money.

The cool thing is anyone can be a leader even if they’re an introvert, neurodivergent, or don’t have Brad Pitt confidence and charisma. You learn this lesson, like I did, by leading small teams.

12. Get to inbox zero every day

Makes you feel better. Makes your to-do list shorter. Forces you to make decisions instead of putting things off.

13. Become a fly on the wall of big deals

My millionaire boss blessed me.

He let me become the lead on a deal with Bryan Johnson’s (don’t-die guy) Braintree. I learned a lot about negotiation and high-stakes situations from this experience. I wasn’t ready to do it, but did it anyway.

If a Google or Apple-style company is doing business with your employer, get in the room. Be the note-taker. Watch the art of the deal. Pay attention to the negotiation.

This skill is how you get on big deals yourself and have a war chest of great stories.

14. Always be early to new technology

When I saw the trend of companies like Stripe becoming unicorns, I got on it.

My fellow colleagues laughed at me. They called me “the brain” for working with Braintree and gave me sh*t. But f*ck them. I was right.

When everyone is pointing out the risk or refusing to change... be the bright light. Go first. Embrace AI. Try new tools. Change processes. Be the catalyst. Management will kiss you on the butt when you do.

15. Become a thought leader in your field

Social media is a powerful way to do it. Get on the company podcast too. And embrace public speaking in your job whenever possible.

I have millions of followers online. I built the following while I worked a job. It set me up for life and allowed me to never work a boring job again. The barrier to entry has never been lower, and AI made it easier.

Build a small following of 5K-10K followers on one platform.

Inspire. Educate. Lead. Entertain.

16. Understand how investing works

My millionaire boss became that way by investing his salary into stocks and startups.

He always saw the salary as an investment fund, not a lifestyle fund. Then he made enough money to make working a job optional. Smart.

I copied him.

I kept my living expenses low, drove a cr*ppy Honda Civic (when all the other bankers had BMWs and Benzes), and I invested in tech stocks and crypto.

After 10 years many of those investments are up over 400%. I didn’t day trade. No. I did deep research, picked obvious long-term winners, then invested and held for 10+ years (not financial advice).

You can too. Doesn’t take a lot of brains.

17. Insist on taking temporary assignments

My millionaire boss helped me get temporary gigs in the social media team and in the innovation lab. This changed my career forever. And it gave me a level of prestige no one could match in interviews where we were competing against each other.

Fill in for someone on holidays. Work in other departments. Be a trial leader. Attend management meetings as a guest.

Being stuck in one department is career death in disguise.

18. Have zero desire to retire.

Employees make this mistake all the time.

They think the goal is to retire and never work again. But that’s a one-way ticket to a boring life that’ll make you miserable. My millionaire boss taught me the real goal should be to retire, so you can go right back to work (like he did).

The difference is when you’ve made decent money and have investments, you play the game differently. You don’t have to work. You choose to work.

And your investments and moderate wealth allow you to say no to people and opportunities you don’t vibe with.

Same happened with me.

I retired at 34 only to go right back to work the next day. The difference is I now do work that doesn’t feel like work and it’s optional. That’s the real goal. That’s modern freedom working how it should.

To retire is to die. Statistically speaking people usually die within a few years of retiring. It's because without work there is no purpose. So the body gets lazy and health starts to decline.

I want to work until I'm dead. The right work is fun and meaningful.

19. Become unemployable.

Working a job is level one. Don't stay stuck there. Get so good at being an entrepreneur in your job that you're unemployable.

Then migrate to level two of your career, which is being a business owner.

Final Thought

My boss went from a salary worker, to a millionaire, to quitting to run his own business. He was a wild guy. Kind of like a Buddhist monk. Wasn't really a boss at all.

He taught me so much. Take what I learned from him and go become wealthy yourself.

I’m here to give you a glimpse of a future that I think none of us expected. It’s a future where AIs are governed by laws, not by programs that try to contain and control them.

First, my secret: I see the future by living in it. I am spending the equivalent of $122k/month of API token spend, or about $4,000 per day, using 21 Claude Max accounts, a number that has been growing steadily at 2 per week. I’m using them to build my video game, Wyvern, which I’ve worked on for 30 years, and now it’s ready to fly.

For ten weeks, I’ve used Claude Fable 5 exclusively for all my design and planning, and also for agents that interface with humans. I have built a team of 18 “officer” seats, all Heads of This and That, all long-lived Fable instances. I also have mostly-headless Sol and Opus fleets, for implementation, reviews, and monitoring. Fable runs them.

I am running an organization of around 50–60 agents, five of whom are interfacing with around 10 humans in the outside world: myself, my 5-person core game design team, my accountant, my chief of staff, and a few others. Only Fable is allowed to talk to humans, via Slack and email.

items.title: Anger, Anxiety and Agency
items.content_html:
Sean Goedecke wrote a post arguing that you should never be angry at work — a post with which I strongly agree. Anger can be a useful signal, but being angry at work rarely improves the situation. More often, it makes life worse for the people around you, many of whom have no more power over the source of your anger than you do. I did learn that lesson, but it did not come naturally. One thing in particular that I learned is that in a company there is a shared vision, and if you don’t agree with it and are not in a position to change it, you should not start a mutiny, not even a small-scale one. Nothing good comes from that.

In the discussion around that topic, one of the most upvoted comments on the Lobsters thread asked a question I had to think about quite a bit:

How can you work in tech right now and not be angry?

In the context of the thread, this was clearly also about AI and agents. For me, the emotions I would expect in tech vis-a-vis these new developments are disorientation and anxiety, but not anger.

Anxiety as an emotion does not require someone to blame. Right now, I find it reasonable to feel anxious about an uncertain future. Who knows what our professions will turn into and what kind of world my kids will find themselves in when they enter the workplace? And if you’ve been in the industry for a long time, will the skills you’ve spent years acquiring still matter?

But anger is different from anxiety because anger needs to be directed somewhere. The feeling of anger suggests that somebody or something is doing something to you.

Who are you going to be angry at and why are you angry in the first place? One narrative that is pretty pervasive is that if AI will usher in productivity gains, those gains are going to benefit companies rather than employees. And well at least someone at Meta wants that. Yet I also find that plenty of people in leadership positions express doubt about AI. They see that an increasing share of their costs is being funneled directly to some large AI labs. They express worries about what will happen to their data and whether these large companies will step into their space instead of being partners.

My answer to the question of how you can not be angry in tech is that it’s by no way the most only possible feeling. First of all, instead of being angry, you can simply be unsure. The feeling of uncertainty is a much more productive emotional state because it can lead to curiosity. Even if you don’t find what’s happening right now exciting, you can at least find it interesting. We have access to magic machines, and we can poke at them and see what happens. The second way is to feel genuine excitement. Once you move beyond curiosity, you can come away with a newfound feeling of power and freedom. A lot of the gains from AI aren’t turning into productivity gains that are reflected in company profits but they’re showing up instead in the number of side projects shipped by everybody not on their company’s time.

The fact that this is happening shows us that owners and founders don’t necessarily know what will happen. Ownership comes with agency, but it does not provide foresight, and this change is disorienting for everybody. I engage with plenty of people who project confidence in public and are much less certain in private. Many of them are placing bets, but they are talking with confidence about those bets, trying to keep their business afloat while the ground moves under them. They experience that uncertainty from a position where they can act on it, and they are often standing somewhere with a megaphone to get others on their side to improve their odds.

I feel that contradiction myself: I am simultaneously tremendously excited, but I am also unsure what will happen next. I do not know what it will mean to be a programmer in the future, and, as the owner of a company, I am also not sure where the high ground will be when this all settles. Much of what I learned over the years is changing rapidly, including ideas I considered fundamental to my craft and business. Some days that feels liberating, but on others I wake up feeling like the ground is crumbling beneath me.

Anxiety is an uncomfortable emotion because it acknowledges that you do not know what will happen and might not be able to stop it. On the other hand, anger can feel more actionable because, instead of saying “I don’t know,” you already have someone to blame. It turns a loss of control into a comforting story with a villain. But I feel that particularly when it comes to AI, it’s easy to pick the wrong villain because of how disruptive the change is for everyone. Your engineering manager or leadership team might themselves feel uncertain about their future and just try to bolster their own confidence by projecting clarity and certainty.

That does not mean there are no villains. When this all plays out, some will profit and many will not. I’m afraid we’re completely ignoring the impact this has on society at large, the climate, and the balance of the world as a whole. As excited as I am about the technology, I worry about Europe’s lack of ambition and growing dependence on other countries. I have a lot of complex thoughts about what we’re doing as an industry right now.

I don’t know what the future of this industry will look like, and I don’t know who will benefit from it and I don’t think I’m alone with that. However I can only urge anyone who feels anger and looks for a villain right to instead remain curious instead. To be curious enough to understand what is changing, excited enough to experiment with it. And then, from what we learn, earn the right to decide when resistance is warranted and where to direct it.

items.title: Fast and Hard Code
items.content_html:
One of the memes on Twitter is that “programming is solved now.” I’m not sure to what degree it is, but one thing is pretty clear: the act of familiarizing yourself with a language no longer matters and some of the friction that mattered for humans does not matter for agents.

As a result, LLMs make language choice much less consequential than it used to be. If you don’t like the choice, you can seemingly rewrite it in another language and you can make it pick a language that you, as a programmer, are entirely unfamiliar with.

Which in turn means that people can, and do, choose based on the marketing of languages much more. As a long-term Rust programmer I found it quite fascinating to see people now ship Rust code who previously might not have chosen it. I attribute at least one part of this to two recent vibe shifts: there is a lot more talk about wanting fast software, and about LLMs being exceptional at optimizing code without regressing behavior.

Folks like Mitchell Hashimoto, Charlie Marsh, Jarred Sumner, Daniel Lemire and quite a few others always carried a certain level of obsession with fast and performant software and they also all happen to be receptive to agents writing code. Maybe as a result, or unrelated others are now joining in. That’s because with things like autoresearch you don’t even necessarily need to know all the tricks: you just need to put an agent on it — though knowledge greatly helps!

If you look around, there are plenty of projects that want to be fast and small, and they increasingly pick “hard languages”. And it’s not just Rust that is benefiting. Even Zig — despite the fact that the creators and parts of the core community are pretty negative on the whole AI thing — is too. For instance Cloudflare’s new Artifacts service uses a pure-Zig Git-protocol engine, compiled to a roughly 100 KB WebAssembly module and Vercel released fx, a Zig coding agent advertised to be small and fast. From what I can tell, all these projects are largely LLM-assisted.

But it’s not just people picking less common languages but also that they are increasingly working with “much harder” technologies. All of a sudden I have seen people do some really impressive stuff with DWARF files, eBPF, custom network drivers, custom crypto and really old computing hardware. Many of these things were previously off-limits for lots of developers. In some cases (eg: crypto) you were even pushed away because those things were intentionally gatekept by the people in the know.

So maybe the world will have more slop, but it might also have more developers in it, that want things to be fast and small.

items.title: How to become someone who actually does sh*t
items.content_html:
Share

I used to be the worst procrastinator. It was embarrassing.

I’m not even sure I want to share this because it’ll take the shine off my BS public image. It may even make me look like an amateur or a wannabe. But a theme of this newsletter is I’m willing to look dumb for your benefit. So here goes…

I used to be full of excuses. I’d think with my d*ck. I never did anything. I had mediocre goals. I’d act short term. My life was directionless. I spent 5 years in call centers because I was full of fear.

In my head there was this version of me that could do better.

That version was technically a fantasy, but I was delusional enough to believe they would one day run my life. I spoke to them in third person too.

There came a point 5 years ago where I’d finally had enough. I was not tapping into my potential and got sick of being underpaid. A mentor I worked with screamed at me and basically told me I was useless.

I’m not alone.

Many people live like this. They have potential but they never actually do sh*t. They just indulge in fantasies and tell people “I have potential, dontcha know.”

The world doesn’t care about your potential.

You’re either already doing things and have proof of work, or you’re ignored. It’s ruthless but that’s how the world works and most people don’t understand this. And I’m not here to sugarcoat it or kiss your ass for empty likes.

I’m now someone who actually does sh*t. I can make a decision to drop $2M in 30 minutes which I could never do before. It’s inspired many people around me to start doing things themselves.

These ideas will help you actually get sh*t done instead of being a daydreamer.

Stay away from these events full of parasites

When I used to work in banking I got told to “network.”

So I’d go to startup events like a junkie. My event of choice was Startup Grind. I’d go there at 7PM with a pocket full of business cards and a $2 smile. I’d sit around and eat canapés with other wannabe entrepreneurs.

After a while I found these startup events repulsive.

They were full of people who had big ideas and talked a big game but never actually did anything. Most of the people were hoping investors would come to the event, so they could pitch their miserable eCommerce startup and get free money.

Many of the attendees accidentally thought I could invest in their startup because I worked in a bank. They were so uneducated they didn’t understand that banks only lend to businesses if they have security (they take your house if you don’t repay the debt, which means you need a house).

I attended these events for 5 years. I no longer go.

Events are full of idea guys and gals. They’re pretenders. They’re procrastinators. Most importantly, networking events are full of amateurs.

Real people who have real results don’t hang out at networking events.

That’s because doers have results and they’re too busy doing to go to a networking event and hand out business cards while jerking off over startup ideas. I retired from going to startup events a long time ago. It gives me time to actually do sh*t.

Networking events are full of parasites. They’re full of people who want to use and abuse you to help them progress their selfish intentions.

The best way to network is to actually build things, then you’ll attract other doers.

Overwhelm equals growth

The average person can’t do things because they’re too easily overwhelmed.

And when they experience overwhelm, they label it as burnout or a mid-life crisis and it goes from being mild to life-threatening.

Most overwhelm is good.

The reframe is that overwhelm leads to growth.

The opposite of overwhelm is comfort. That’s how most people drown and waste decades of their life. If you only do easy things or subconsciously choose paths that contain zero discomfort, you won’t do anything notable. It gets worse…

Too much comfort leads to boredom. It robs you of the joy of uncertainty. And so you die at 25 and get buried at 75. It’s a slow death. Overwhelm is actually better than an orga$m. It’s how you produce idea babies and do something that changes the world in some small way.

If you’re not overwhelmed at least once a week, something is likely wrong.

Reframe overwhelm as a positive opportunity, and you’ll finally start getting more things done. Society has got to stop calling everything burnout because it’s producing millions of useless, unproductive cowards that AI is primed to replace.

Master the incredible power of neuroplasticity

Self-improvement is bullsh*t. Neuroplasticity proves it.

Your brain doesn’t care about your goals, your intentions, or your Lambo vision board. It’s running one question on a loop: “What should I get better at?” And it answers based on what you actually do, not what you want. That’s neuroplasticity in action, wiring itself around your behavior whether you like it or not.

Stop wanting outcomes. Start repeating behaviors.

Want to be fit? Show your brain what a fit person does every day and neuroplasticity will rewire it around that, whether you “feel motivated” or not.

I did this with writing. I didn’t sit around dreaming about being an author — I wrote online every single day and published over 7,000 essays. That repetition is what got me a book deal with Penguin, not the goal.

Wanting isn’t the mechanism. Repeating is.

Once you understand neuroplasticity, you stop chasing outcomes and start engineering behavior — because that’s the only thing your brain is listening to.

Worship systems like they’re your Jesus

People who get sh*t done don’t guess or wing it.

They don’t go it alone with trial and error and end up frustrated and then quit. No. People who do sh*t rely on systems. They know that if they don’t systemize it, then the task isn’t repeatable, and they can’t outsource the work later on either.

Systems are now even more important because you can train AI to complete and run low-level systems for you that saves you a heap of time.

I had someone tell me yesterday on Threads “AI is evil and you shouldn’t endorse it. People still do things without AI dontcha know.”

No they don’t. AI is everywhere. These same people are already using AI and don’t even realize it because it’s in most software.

Don’t hate AI.

This is low IQ. Understand the pros and cons and use AI to build systems that make you the Jesus of your field.

Turn hard problems into easy problems in your head

Tim Ferriss is not my guru. But he says some clever stuff.

His mantra is “What would this look like if it were easy?” The tendency is to overthink hard problems or big tasks which prevents you from taking action.

I take hard problems and ask myself what the easiest version would be to solve it. That means stripping away all of Timmy-Time’s perfectionism and the 101 steps, and just starting with the bare minimum.

I recently wanted to change accountants. It’s a big project. I didn’t wanna do it. So I turned it into easy mode by only agreeing to have one meeting with one accountant.

This made it easier. The meeting went well. The next step was small. For 3 months I worked my way through each small step and eventually signed the contract. This is how you take giant projects and make them actionable.

Being too big picture is a nightmare that’ll give you herpes.

Stop waiting for the right time or for the chaos to pass

Mental model: it’s never the right time to do anything.

You will never feel ready. You will never have 100% certainty. There are zero guarantees in life other than you will die and pay taxes. You could be dead tomorrow so the only right time is today while your heart is still beating.

The reason you wait for the right time is because your brain creates these fantasies that one day in the future the chaos will calm down and you’ll be free to think clearly and make your move. This is a XXX p0rn movie.

Chaos never goes away.

People die. You get sick. Babies will be born. Marriages can end in divorce. Investments blow up. Houses get broken into. And clumsy people like me fall over in the gym and injure their leg because we think we’re Rocky Balboa.

The chaos never passes. The universe runs on entropy. Chaos is hard-wired into mother nature. We need chaos AND order for the world to function. So if you’re hoping for no chaos, you’re hoping to live a life no human ever experiences. Are you an alien from Mars here to give me an anal probe? (Joking not joking).

Learn to expect chaos. Learn to thrive in chaos. See chaos as an opportunity rather than a threat that’ll stab you in the heart and murder your firstborn baby.

Mental model: Do it today, never tomorrow.

If you’re not going to do it today, it’s a pure fantasy. Don’t indulge.

Chunk everything down into stupidly small steps

How a goal looks and feels in your head is enough to stop you doing sh*t.

The default is for your brain to overthink and exaggerate every problem you’re trying to solve in life to protect you from predators. The antidote is to chunk problems down. Break the goal down into small steps.

For example, I help people build digital businesses. That feels scary and big. I overcome the problem by turning a business into a set of small actions with KPIs. Post content, build email list, have conversations, make offers – stuff like that.

If you’re not already chunking down every action you need to take to achieve a goal, start doing it. It’ll help you make a lot more progress. I often ask “What’s the smallest step I could take right now?”

Not the biggest step. Not the highest ROI step. Not the smartest step. Not the step I most want to do. THE SMALLEST STEP.

This is how you get out of your own way.

Controversial truth: You’re the biggest roadblock to actually getting stuff done

Being obsessed with the external factors holds people back.

It’s not the market, the customer who didn’t sign the contract, the lowering of interest rates, or the market adoption that’s stopping you from making stuff happen.

No. 99.9% of the time you’re the reason sh*t isn’t being done.

You’re the biggest problem which is also a huge opportunity because you have complete control to fix that.

Most people don’t get stuff done because their psychology prevents them from thinking about problems, action, and ROI in the right way.

So they stand in their own way and overthink and overanalyze everything, then always come back to the same logical conclusion in their mind. But these logical conclusions are logical to them, and illogical to anyone other than them.

The smartest, most highly credentialed, most high IQ person doesn’t get sh*t done. Read that ten times.

So-called smart people are so smart they talk themselves out of every good opportunity because they don’t actually do sh*t to see if the opportunity is good. They assume they can vet an opportunity by thinking through it which you can’t.

As the meme goes, an idiot in motion will always go further than a genius at rest. Get in motion. Do sh*t. Any sh*t. Just don’t sit there in your head thinking you’re going to outsmart the power of momentum that comes with action.

Once you get moving you figure out what you need to do.

And whatever you start out thinking you need to do will almost certainly be wrong. So if you can’t predict, plan, or strategize what is going to happen, then what do ya do, man? You act.

You act ruthlessly with a level of execution that makes you look like a psycho. Then your friends say “You’ve changed, man” and you end up being best friends with Youtuber Mr Beast and celebrate with chocolate cake. You feel me?

Believe in yourself, Scotty

This is where I get a little biblical.

You gotta believe in yourself. I know…corny as hell. Here’s what I mean: if you don’t believe in yourself, you’ll never go all in. You’ll keep hedging your bets and making pissy moves that get you nowhere.

When you don’t believe in yourself you end up sabotaging yourself and your every move. This leads you to act like a coward which becomes a massive lack of focus.

Do the opposite. The cool kids now call this delusional optimism. It means act as if you will succeed and you’re highly likely to find a way to make it happen.

Understand the important role of dopamine

Dopamine is a form of her0in for most people.

They chase things that give them dopamine:

  • Information collecting

  • Making plans

  • Going to events

  • Buying equipment

  • Designing logos

  • Telling people about their goals

  • Collecting credentials

  • Doing podcast interviews

Even eating junk food produces dopamine. Watching Netflix does too. And your brain loves dopamine. It craves it. So when you do too many dopamine-producing activities, you give the brain a sugar high.

But then comes the slump. Then comes the dopamine addiction. And before you know it, you’re looking at your phone most of the day because it’s the biggest producer of dopamine in history.

If you overindulge in dopamine, it goes from being a subtle creator of human motivation to completely hijacking your brain’s reward system

You may as well be a crack addict. There’s not much difference.

The antidote is to swap out the artificial forms of dopamine and naturally produce it by doing sh*t, getting results, achieving goals, and doing real work.

Understand this one idea, and you’ll be ahead of 99% of people.

Closing Thought

Most people don’t do sh*t.

They get to the end of their lives and end up with regrets. They tell people about their potential rather than what they’ve done.

They indulge in mental gymnastics for decades trying to outsmart the laws of the universe, the laws of science and momentum, and the last few hundred years that shows action-takers get paid a lot more money than everyone else.

I won’t copy Nike and say “Just do it.” (Or will I?)

I’ll leave you with this. You already have the talent, enough information, enough expertise, enough time, and enough skills.

What you need to do is rewire your brain using neuroplasticity to become someone who behaves like a person that actually gets sh*t done. That’s it. Behavior leads to action. Action leads to results. Results create momentum. Momentum builds confidence. And quiet confidence makes you undeniable.

Light the self-improvement books on fire. You got this.

P.S.

Top of the list of sh*t people never do is make $10,000 in a single month.

Is this possible?

Yes.

How?

Because making $10,000 in 30 days is not an effort problem but a business model problem.

If you’re ready to stop procrastinating and hit your first $10,000 month, head to this page and read carefully.

items.title: What Is Reasoning
items.content_html:
A few weeks ago a paper was shared that showed how to extract reasoning traces from closed-weight models. Together with online discussions about tricking models into leaking them, it made me investigate it more out of curiosity. Twitter seems full of half-truths and confusion about how this works, so perhaps this helps some to understand what is happening.

Hiding Traces

Reasoning traces are usually hidden from us. We have lamented this, but mostly have to accept it. Open-weight models thankfully reveal them, and from their behavior you can see that their traces can be long and confusing. This is probably a good reason to separate them from what is normally shown to users.

At minimum, UIs need to detect them. The industry has done a good job at making reasoning traces sound special and exotic, but they really are just text: the model is trained to emit its thinking into a scratchpad as part of its response, before its final answer.

GPT-OSS’s Harmony response format makes this easy to see:

<|channel|>analysis<|message|>
I need to work this out ...
<|end|><|start|>assistant<|channel|>final<|message|>
The answer is ...
<|return|>

The markers are special tokens, but the reasoning between them uses “the same text” as the final answer (just that GPT chain-of-thought text sounds really funny). When the model samples the analysis channel token, a parser routes the following text into a separate stream exposed through the Responses API. For closed models, presumably a simple model redacts and summarizes it.

Reasoning Effort

How much budget goes to reasoning? Earlier APIs exposed reasoning token budgets, making it seem like a property of the sampling process. In reality, reasoning effort is baked into the system prompt. GPT-OSS puts this into the system prompt:

Reasoning: low

That’s it. Training produces the resulting behavior, such as emitting the token sequence that switches to the analysis channel. This also explains why changing the effort invalidates the KV cache. I think closed GPT models call reasoning effort “juice,” since you can ask most models how much juice they have.

In DwarfStar for DeepSeek with max reasoning this is added to the system prompt:

Reasoning Effort: Absolute maximum with no shortcuts permitted.
You MUST be very thorough in your thinking and comprehensively decompose the
problem to resolve the root cause, rigorously stress-testing your logic against
all potential paths, edge cases, and adversarial scenarios.

Don’t Think

The destination of reasoning tokens is therefore a learned convention: the model is trained to keep scratch work out of the final channel. Trick it into thinking it is in that channel and it may leak tokens. We have even seen older models, when thinking is disabled, reason into the bash tool and echo their thoughts to /dev/null.

So in some sense the only “special” behavior for some models is not to think. That at times is done by “mechanically” removing the model’s usual ways to think. In DwarfStar, disabled thinking uses the prefill </think>, while enabled thinking uses <think>, which are the tokens that close and start thinking. GPT-OSS doesn’t prefill but lets the model decide either way on its own.

But presumably, some inference APIs prefill the opening token when reasoning is enabled, so the model never samples it itself and might prevent the sampling of the reasoning token when disabled since it can be trivially detected. This may explain why a custom think tool can trick models into putting some reasoning where it should not go — but only when native reasoning is disabled.

Fun fact: this blog post triggered safey checks

items.title: Opus 5 doesn't use em-dashes in code comments
items.content_html:
I’ve been using Opus 5 as my main coding for the last few days 1, and I noticed something odd: the code comments stopped using em-dashes; everything is double hyphens (--) now.

Instead of going off a gut feeling, I decided to actually run some checks. agentsview indexes all my conversations into a SQLite database, so this kind of question is just a query away. Here’s the chart:

Seems pretty clear to me! But you might say “maybe it’s not the model, maybe it’s something else”.

Well actually the cleanest evidence came from a session where I switched from Fable to Opus 5 mid-conversation and didn’t touch anything else. Looking at just that session, Fable produced 11 em-dashes in comments. Opus 5 produced 36 double hyphens. I didn’t touch anything else.

What I find genuinely strange is that this only affects code comments. My chat replies still have just as many em-dashes as ever. So maybe something was tweaked when training for code-generation in particular?
